opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me start with why I think it's necessary.

**Why it's necessary**

If you take AGI seriously, meaning a system that can do what a capable human researcher does, then it has to be able to do science. It has to form hypotheses, design experiments, run them, look at the results, and revise its beliefs. That loop is the core of intelligence in an open-ended world.

A system that only answers questions within the distribution of its training data, however impressively, isn't general in the sense I care about. It's general in breadth but not in depth, because it can't push the frontier.

So auto-research, or AI that does science, is a kind of litmus test. If a system can't do research autonomously, I would be hesitant to call it AGI. There's also a practical side. If we want AI to accelerate progress in physics, biology, or AI itself, research ability is exactly the capability that compounds. That's why I think of it as necessary.

**Why it's insufficient**

Research is one specific mode of intelligence. It's very goal-directed: there's a question, and you try to resolve it. A lot of what we mean by general intelligence lives outside that frame:

- **Choosing what's worth asking.** Good researchers have taste. They have some sense of which problems matter, which are tractable, and which are beautiful. That taste is shaped by values, aesthetics, and lived experience. Current auto-research pipelines mostly optimize within a problem someone already framed. Being good at executing research is not the same as being good at deciding what research to do.
- **Embodiment and interaction with the physical world.** Much of science is messy. You build apparatus, things break, and you notice something weird out of the corner of your eye. A system that only operates on text and code, even if it writes papers, misses a big part of that. You could have a superb theorist that is still quite limited as an agent in the world.
- **Social and long-horizon intelligence.** Science is a collective activity. You persuade people, collaborate, and maintain a research program over years while your understanding gradually deepens. Today's systems are good at short bursts but struggle with coherent long-horizon agency and building up a stable understanding over time.
- **Understanding, not just results.** This is the point I care about most, coming from interpretability and physics. A system could find correct results, like fitting a formula or discovering a better architecture, without anything we'd call understanding. I think real intelligence involves compressing knowledge into concepts you can reuse, transfer, and reason with. If auto-research produces results without that conceptual compression, it's useful but brittle. It looks like science from the outside without fully being science on the inside.

**Putting it together**

I'd say auto-research is a very good benchmark and a very powerful capability, maybe the most economically and scientifically impactful one. But passing it doesn't certify generality. It's like saying a good mathematician must be intelligent, which is true, but intelligence isn't only mathematics.

For me the interesting open question is whether pursuing auto-research will force us to solve the other pieces, like taste, understanding, and long-horizon agency, or whether we'll get systems that are very good research tools while those deeper parts remain missing. My guess is that, at least in the near term, it's the latter. That's why I keep emphasizing that we should care about understanding, not just performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd start by saying the phrase "AI for AI," or auto-research, has become something of a slogan recently, and I think the slogan hides an important asymmetry.

The "necessary" part is easy to argue. If you look at how progress in AI has actually happened over the past decade, the bottleneck has not been compute alone, and it has not been data alone. It has been the number of good ideas tried per unit time. A research lab is essentially a search process: you propose an architecture tweak, an optimizer change, a data recipe, you run it, you read the loss curve, you update your beliefs, and you go again. Humans are slow at this loop. We sleep, we get attached to our own hypotheses, we have maybe a few dozen serious experiments in us per year. If you want to get to systems that are qualitatively more capable than today's, I don't think you can get there with human-paced iteration. So you need the machine in the loop, not just as a tool but as the thing generating and testing hypotheses. In that sense I'm fully on board. Any path to AGI almost certainly passes through AI doing a large fraction of AI research.

The "insufficient" part is where I think people get too optimistic, and it comes from my own experience doing science, both in physics and in interpretability. Auto-research, as it exists now, is very good at optimizing within a space that has already been defined. You give it a benchmark, a search space, a metric, and it will find things in that space faster than you can. But almost every real breakthrough I can think of came from someone realizing the space itself was wrong. The metric was measuring the wrong thing, or the right question hadn't been asked yet. When we did KAN, for example, the interesting part wasn't searching over architectures. It was stepping back and asking why we treat the activation function as fixed and the weights as learned, rather than the other way around. That's a reframing, not a search. I don't yet see evidence that current systems do that kind of move reliably, because it requires having a model of what you don't understand, which is exactly the thing that's hard to write down as an objective.

There's also a more subtle issue, which is that auto-research tends to amplify whatever it is given. If the evaluation suite is biased toward a certain kind of capability, say pattern completion on text, you get a system that becomes extremely good at that and tells you it's making progress, and you may be moving very fast in a direction that doesn't lead to general intelligence at all. Speed without the right direction is not progress, it's just faster drift. And the faster the loop, the less time humans have to notice the drift.

So my view is that AFAI is the engine, but it's not the steering. The steering still comes from understanding, from science in the old-fashioned sense: building compact, mechanistic explanations of why these systems work, where they fail, and what intelligence actually requires. That's why I keep insisting on interpretability and on physics-style thinking even when it looks slow and unfashionable. The engine will get built regardless, the incentives guarantee it. The question is whether we understand enough to point it somewhere worth going.

astra-6.text:
I think auto-research is necessary because an AGI should be able to discover things that we don’t already know. It should formulate hypotheses, test them, learn from failures, and improve its understanding without a human specifying every step.

But that’s only one part of intelligence. You can automate a research process while still having humans choose the problem, define what counts as success, and provide the framework for evaluating results. The system might be very capable within that framework, yet struggle when the framework itself needs to change.

So the distinction is between solving a given problem and figuring out what problem to solve—and whether you’re even asking the right question. Auto-research is an important capability, but demonstrating it alone doesn’t establish the flexibility and breadth we would want from AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I see auto-research as necessary because an AGI should be able to generate new knowledge, not just reproduce what humans already know. It needs to ask questions, form hypotheses, run experiments, and learn from the results. Automating that process is a very important step.

But it’s insufficient because doing research is only part of intelligence. You can imagine a system that is extremely good at solving a well-defined research problem, while still depending on humans to decide which problems matter, choose the right assumptions, and interpret the results. That would be a powerful researcher, but it wouldn’t automatically be a general intelligence.

The distinction is between closing a research loop and being able to decide what loop to build. If we give a system an objective and an evaluation metric, it may make tremendous progress within that setup. But can it recognize when the setup itself is wrong? Can it introduce a new concept, transfer its understanding to an unfamiliar situation, or decide that a different question is more useful? Those are additional capabilities we need to understand.

So I think auto-research is an essential capability and a useful testing ground. But we shouldn’t assume that making research autonomous, by itself, solves the whole problem of general intelligence.
